metadata.narrative: I am a software engineer at a small startup, trying to scale our product to around 1M users / day from around the world. The service is a social media app similar to twitter, where users can write a message and follow others. Right now we have a simple web interface with a local mySQL database. Please write a technical report on the transition to more scaled software and provide recommendations for anything you consider a necessary change.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Scaling a Twitter-like platform from a single-region web app backed by one local MySQL instance to about one million users per day worldwide requires rethinking storage, caching, messaging, deployment topology, and security together.

Capacity planning should start from realistic numbers, and Twitter's own published figures are a useful proxy: at 150 million active users the platform saw about 300,000 read requests per second for timelines against only about 5,000 new posts per second written, a roughly 60-to-1 read-to-write ratio that should guide where engineering effort goes first.

That same analysis shows Twitter deliberately chose eventual consistency for timelines and set explicit service-level objectives, such as 99.5 percent of timelines loading within 500 milliseconds, rather than demanding strict consistency everywhere.
A startup with a similar workload shape should adopt the same posture: optimize aggressively for the read path and accept eventual consistency for feed ordering.

A single local MySQL server cannot survive this transition unmodified, and the practical playbook is incremental: separate the web and database tiers so they scale independently, introduce read replicas to offload the primary, and only move to full sharding once replica capacity is exhausted.

MySQL specifically supports this path through read replicas, table partitioning, functional partitioning of databases by feature area, and eventually horizontal sharding by a key such as user ID, and managed services like Amazon RDS or Google Cloud SQL can absorb much of the operational burden.

However, read replicas are not a free scaling lever: all writes still funnel through a single master, which remains a bottleneck, and asynchronous replication introduces lag so a user's own write may not be visible on a replica immediately afterward, a problem typically solved by forcing a user's own reads back to the primary or polling the replica until the write appears.

Read replicas also break monotonic-read consistency, since a client can bounce between replicas and see the database move backward in time, and because each replica must hold the entire working set, replicas scale read throughput but not necessarily read latency once data no longer fits in memory.

When volume outgrows replication, true partitioning becomes necessary, and the available schemes include vertical partitioning by feature, range partitioning by value, hash-based partitioning by user ID, and directory-based partitioning through a lookup service, each trading off rebalancing difficulty against the loss of cross-shard joins, which forces denormalizing data such as user profiles and posts together.

Because a social feed is fundamentally a fan-out problem rather than a relational-join problem, the architecture should separate post storage from timeline storage entirely: writes trigger a fanout process that looks up a user's followers and pushes the new post's ID into each follower's precomputed timeline, held in an in-memory store rather than recomputed from joins on every read.

In practice this means storing only compact identifiers, such as post ID, author ID, and small metadata, in a Redis structure capped to a bounded number of recent items per timeline, replicated across machines for durability and coordinated through a system like Zookeeper.

This fanout-on-write approach should be decoupled from the request path using a message queue such as Kafka, whose topics and partitions let fanout workers scale horizontally across brokers independent of the web tier, and whose durable log also supports migrating pieces of a growing codebase into separate services later.

Caching deserves a layered strategy beyond timelines: an in-memory layer such as Memcached or Redis should sit in front of the database for hot reads, but as Facebook's experience shows, a large cache fleet introduces problems like incast congestion when many web servers fan out requests to many cache servers at once, so client-side coalescing and stale-value tolerance matter as much as the cache itself.

A global content delivery network should serve static and semi-static assets from edge servers near each user, reducing origin load and latency while absorbing traffic spikes and filtering malicious traffic.

User-uploaded media should move out of the database into object storage like Amazon S3, which offers tiered storage classes, multipart upload for large files, and pre-signed URLs for controlling access to private media.

If keyword or hashtag search becomes a requirement, a dedicated engine such as Elasticsearch, which indexes every field for fast retrieval and is proven at the scale of Netflix and Walmart, should sit alongside the primary datastore rather than being bolted onto MySQL.

Serving a global user base means the web tier must become horizontally scalable, which requires making servers stateless by moving session data into a shared store, so a load balancer can route any request to any server without forcing repeated logins.

For users spread across continents, a single-region database becomes a latency and availability liability, and the recommended pattern is an active-active multi-region database, such as Cassandra-based deployments, that accepts reads and writes in every region, supports disaster recovery when a region fails, and can satisfy data-sovereignty rules like GDPR by pinning certain data to specific geographies while replicating less sensitive data globally.

On splitting the codebase, resist microservices as a default choice this early, since real-world experience shows early-stage startups paying that complexity tax often see slower iteration, poorly defined data domains, and heavy new operational overhead for benefits they do not yet need.

The better rule is to keep a well-factored monolith until a specific subsystem, most likely the fanout and timeline pipeline given the numbers above, clearly outgrows it, and migrate that piece only when the return on investment is demonstrable, following the path Twitter itself took from its Ruby on Rails monolith toward a service-oriented architecture over several years.

Finally, security and visibility cannot be an afterthought: an API gateway should centralize authentication, enforce HTTPS everywhere, apply rate limiting to blunt abuse and denial-of-service traffic, and forward access logs to a monitoring system, ideally paired with a web application firewall for defense in depth.

As the system grows into more independent services, monitoring tools like Prometheus and Grafana should track per-service health metrics while distributed tracing tools like Jaeger and centralized logging provide the observability needed to find which service caused a failure in a request that touched many of them.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

tools.name: search
tools.description: Search the available evidence corpus. Results contain ranked document IDs and document text; inspect that text directly and cite by docid. Each result is bounded independently before it is staged.

query.description: A natural-language query for evidence relevant to the research request.

k.description: Number of fused passages to return (default 10).

budget_tokens_per_result.description: Maximum approximate tokens staged per result. Text is bounded at tokens × 5 characters and cut at the final line break before that boundary. Default 4096.

tools.name: commit_context
tools.description: Select the small subset of documents from the MOST RECENT staged search batch whose full text should persist. documents.description: Evidence-worthy staged documents to retain. An empty array explicitly rejects the whole staged batch.

reason.description: The distinct evidence, claim, perspective, date, name, counter-evidence, or coverage area this document uniquely contributes.

Scaling a Twitter-like social platform from a single-region web app backed by one local MySQL instance to roughly one million users per day worldwide requires rethinking nearly every layer of the stack, from data storage through caching, messaging, deployment topology, and security.

The first step is capacity planning grounded in realistic numbers, and Twitter's own published figures are a useful proxy: at 150 million active users the platform saw about 300,000 read requests per second for timeline queries against only about 5,000 new tweets per second written, a roughly 60-to-1 read-to-write ratio that should guide where engineering effort goes first.
[shard_05895_78239]
That same analysis shows Twitter deliberately chose eventual consistency for timelines and set explicit service-level objectives, such as 99.5 percent of timelines loading within 500 milliseconds, rather than demanding strict consistency everywhere.
[shard_05895_78239]
A startup targeting a similar workload shape should adopt the same posture: optimize aggressively for the read path, and accept eventual consistency for non-critical data like feed ordering.

On the database itself, a single local MySQL server cannot survive this transition unmodified, and the practical playbook is incremental: first separate the web and database tiers so they scale independently, then introduce read replicas to offload query load from the primary, and only move to full sharding once replica capacity is exhausted.
[shard_02633_40268]
[shard_02636_49214]
MySQL specifically supports this path through read replicas, table partitioning, functional partitioning of databases by feature area, and eventually horizontal sharding by a key such as user ID, and managed services like Amazon RDS or Google Cloud SQL can absorb much of the operational burden of running this fleet.
[shard_02636_49214]
However, read replicas are not a free scaling lever: all writes still funnel through a single master, which remains a bottleneck, and asynchronous replication introduces lag so that a user's own write may not be visible on a replica immediately afterward.
[shard_00047_14200]
This read-after-write problem is real in production, and common fixes include forcing a user's own reads back to the primary immediately after a write, or having the application poll the replica and retry until the freshly written row appears.
[shard_02981_18730]
Read replicas also break monotonic-read consistency, since a load-balanced client can bounce between replicas and see the database state move backward in time, and because each replica's cache must hold the entire working set rather than a shard of it, replicas scale read throughput but not necessarily read latency once the data no longer fits in memory.
[shard_06109_52630]
When query volume or data volume outgrows what replication can address, true partitioning becomes necessary, and the available schemes include vertical partitioning by feature, range partitioning by value, hash-based partitioning by user ID, and directory-based partitioning through a lookup service, each with tradeoffs in rebalancing difficulty and the loss of cross-shard joins that will require denormalizing data such as user profiles and posts together.
[shard_04535_538]

Because a social feed is fundamentally a fan-out problem rather than a relational-join problem, the architecture should separate tweet storage from timeline storage entirely, following the pattern used by large-scale platforms: writes trigger a fanout process that looks up a user's followers and pushes the new post's ID into each follower's precomputed timeline, which lives in an in-memory store rather than being recomputed from joins on every read.
[shard_00252_39492]
[shard_01014_68546]
In practice this means storing only compact identifiers, such as tweet ID, author ID, and a small amount of metadata, in a Redis structure capped to a bounded number of recent items per user's timeline, replicated across multiple machines for durability and coordinated through a system like Zookeeper.
[shard_01014_68546]
[shard_00252_39492]
This fanout-on-write approach should be decoupled from the request path using a message queue such as Kafka, whose topics and partitions let the fanout workers scale horizontally across brokers independent of the web tier, and whose durable log also cleanly supports migrating pieces of a growing codebase into separate services over time.
[shard_02046_26492]

Caching more broadly deserves a layered strategy beyond just timelines: an in-memory layer such as Memcached or Redis should sit in front of the database for hot reads, but as Facebook's experience shows, a large cache fleet introduces its own problems like incast congestion when many web servers fan out requests to many cache servers simultaneously, so client-side request coalescing and stale-value tolerance mechanisms matter as much as the cache itself.
[shard_01866_16499]
A global content delivery network should handle static and semi-static assets, such as profile images and cached API responses, by serving them from edge servers near each user, which reduces origin load and latency while also absorbing traffic spikes and filtering malicious traffic before it reaches the origin.
[shard_01518_74463]
User-uploaded media such as images and video should move out of the database entirely and into object storage like Amazon S3, which offers tiered storage classes, multipart upload for large files, and pre-signed URLs for controlling who can access private media.
[shard_04728_73523]
If keyword or hashtag search becomes a product requirement, a dedicated search engine such as Elasticsearch, which indexes every field for fast retrieval and has been proven at the scale of companies like Netflix and Walmart, should sit alongside the primary datastore rather than being bolted onto MySQL.
[shard_00972_26988]

Serving a global user base also means the web tier itself must become horizontally scalable, which requires making servers stateless by moving session data out of local memory and into a shared store, so that a load balancer can route any request to any server without forcing repeated logins.
[shard_02089_53499]
For users spread across continents, a single-region database becomes a latency and availability liability, and the recommended pattern is an active-active multi-region database, such as Cassandra-based deployments, that accepts reads and writes in every region, supports disaster recovery when a region fails, and can satisfy data-sovereignty rules like GDPR by pinning certain user data to specific geographies while replicating less sensitive data globally.
[shard_00804_17823]

On the question of splitting the codebase, resist microservices as a default choice this early, since real-world experience shows that early-stage startups paying that complexity tax often see slower iteration, poorly defined data domains, and heavy new operational overhead for benefits they do not yet need.
[shard_00820_24153]
The better rule is to keep a well-factored monolith until a specific subsystem, most likely the fanout and timeline pipeline given the numbers above, clearly outgrows it, and to migrate that piece only when the return on investment is demonstrable, following the same evolutionary path Twitter itself took from its Ruby on Rails monolith toward a service-oriented architecture over several years.
[shard_05200_21963]
[shard_06133_7639]

Finally, security and visibility cannot be an afterthought at this scale: an API gateway should centralize authentication, enforce HTTPS everywhere, apply rate limiting to blunt both abuse and distributed denial-of-service traffic, and forward access logs to a monitoring system, ideally paired with a web application firewall for defense in depth.
[shard_02120_81761]
As the system grows into more independent services, monitoring tools like Prometheus and Grafana should track per-service health metrics while distributed tracing tools like Jaeger and centralized logging provide the observability needed to find which specific service caused a failure in a request that touched many of them.

answer.text: Scaling a Twitter-like platform from a single-region web app backed by one local MySQL instance to about one million users per day worldwide requires rethinking storage, caching, messaging, deployment topology, and security together.

Capacity planning should start from realistic numbers, and Twitter's own published figures are a useful proxy: at 150 million active users the platform saw about 300,000 read requests per second for timelines against only about 5,000 new posts per second written, a roughly 60-to-1 read-to-write ratio that should guide where engineering effort goes first.

That same analysis shows Twitter deliberately chose eventual consistency for timelines and set explicit service-level objectives, such as 99.5 percent of timelines loading within 500 milliseconds, rather than demanding strict consistency everywhere.
A startup with a similar workload shape should adopt the same posture: optimize aggressively for the read path and accept eventual consistency for feed ordering.

A single local MySQL server cannot survive this transition unmodified, and the practical playbook is incremental: separate the web and database tiers so they scale independently, introduce read replicas to offload the primary, and only move to full sharding once replica capacity is exhausted.

MySQL specifically supports this path through read replicas, table partitioning, functional partitioning of databases by feature area, and eventually horizontal sharding by a key such as user ID, and managed services like Amazon RDS or Google Cloud SQL can absorb much of the operational burden.

However, read replicas are not a free scaling lever: all writes still funnel through a single master, which remains a bottleneck, and asynchronous replication introduces lag so a user's own write may not be visible on a replica immediately afterward, a problem typically solved by forcing a user's own reads back to the primary or polling the replica until the write appears.

Read replicas also break monotonic-read consistency, since a client can bounce between replicas and see the database move backward in time, and because each replica must hold the entire working set, replicas scale read throughput but not necessarily read latency once data no longer fits in memory.

When volume outgrows replication, true partitioning becomes necessary, and the available schemes include vertical partitioning by feature, range partitioning by value, hash-based partitioning by user ID, and directory-based partitioning through a lookup service, each trading off rebalancing difficulty against the loss of cross-shard joins, which forces denormalizing data such as user profiles and posts together.

Because a social feed is fundamentally a fan-out problem rather than a relational-join problem, the architecture should separate post storage from timeline storage entirely: writes trigger a fanout process that looks up a user's followers and pushes the new post's ID into each follower's precomputed timeline, held in an in-memory store rather than recomputed from joins on every read.

In practice this means storing only compact identifiers, such as post ID, author ID, and small metadata, in a Redis structure capped to a bounded number of recent items per timeline, replicated across machines for durability and coordinated through a system like Zookeeper.

This fanout-on-write approach should be decoupled from the request path using a message queue such as Kafka, whose topics and partitions let fanout workers scale horizontally across brokers independent of the web tier, and whose durable log also supports migrating pieces of a growing codebase into separate services later.

Caching deserves a layered strategy beyond timelines: an in-memory layer such as Memcached or Redis should sit in front of the database for hot reads, but as Facebook's experience shows, a large cache fleet introduces problems like incast congestion when many web servers fan out requests to many cache servers at once, so client-side coalescing and stale-value tolerance matter as much as the cache itself.

A global content delivery network should serve static and semi-static assets from edge servers near each user, reducing origin load and latency while absorbing traffic spikes and filtering malicious traffic.

User-uploaded media should move out of the database into object storage like Amazon S3, which offers tiered storage classes, multipart upload for large files, and pre-signed URLs for controlling access to private media.

If keyword or hashtag search becomes a requirement, a dedicated engine such as Elasticsearch, which indexes every field for fast retrieval and is proven at the scale of Netflix and Walmart, should sit alongside the primary datastore rather than being bolted onto MySQL.

Serving a global user base means the web tier must become horizontally scalable, which requires making servers stateless by moving session data into a shared store, so a load balancer can route any request to any server without forcing repeated logins.

For users spread across continents, a single-region database becomes a latency and availability liability, and the recommended pattern is an active-active multi-region database, such as Cassandra-based deployments, that accepts reads and writes in every region, supports disaster recovery when a region fails, and can satisfy data-sovereignty rules like GDPR by pinning certain data to specific geographies while replicating less sensitive data globally.

On splitting the codebase, resist microservices as a default choice this early, since real-world experience shows early-stage startups paying that complexity tax often see slower iteration, poorly defined data domains, and heavy new operational overhead for benefits they do not yet need.

The better rule is to keep a well-factored monolith until a specific subsystem, most likely the fanout and timeline pipeline given the numbers above, clearly outgrows it, and migrate that piece only when the return on investment is demonstrable, following the path Twitter itself took from its Ruby on Rails monolith toward a service-oriented architecture over several years.

Finally, security and visibility cannot be an afterthought: an API gateway should centralize authentication, enforce HTTPS everywhere, apply rate limiting to blunt abuse and denial-of-service traffic, and forward access logs to a monitoring system, ideally paired with a web application firewall for defense in depth.

As the system grows into more independent services, monitoring tools like Prometheus and Grafana should track per-service health metrics while distributed tracing tools like Jaeger and centralized logging provide the observability needed to find which service caused a failure in a request that touched many of them.
